inverse_theorem.hypothesis: For fixed 0<alpha<1 and eta>0, f_N is a real T3 trigonometric polynomial supported in |k|_2<=N and H_(alpha,N)(sgn f_N)>=eta
inverse_theorem.quartic_control: With delta_N=int(f_N^2-1)^2 and q_N=int f_N^2, |q_N-1|<=sqrt(delta_N) and ||f_N||_4^4=delta_N+2q_N-1<=(1+sqrt(delta_N))^2
inverse_theorem.gradient_control: For delta_N<=1, the L4 trigonometric Bernstein inequality gives ||grad f_N||_4<=C N||f_N||_4<=C N; this is stronger for transition volume than passing through the L-infinity Nikolskii bound
inverse_theorem.coarea_lower_bound: K1548 gives both cores {f_N>=1/2} and {f_N<=-1/2} volume at least eta/8 when delta_N<=9eta/128; relative torus isoperimetry and coarea then give int_(|f_N|<1/2)|grad f_N|>=I_eta>0
inverse_theorem.transition_volume: Holder on the transition set gives I_eta<=int_B|grad f_N|<=mu(B)^(3/4)||grad f_N||_4<=C N mu(B)^(3/4), hence mu(B)>=c_eta N^(-4/3); the defect density is at least 9/16 there
inverse_theorem.conclusion: For every N>=1, delta_N>=c_(alpha,eta) N^(-4/3); the complementary cases delta_N>min(1,9eta/128) satisfy the same bound after reducing the constant
inverse_theorem.scope_guard: The exponent 4/3 is a rigorous three-dimensional inverse bound from L4 defect control, coarea and L4 Bernstein, not a claimed sharp nodal exponent; it requires nonvanishing fixed-ratio sign-shell mass and does not apply to merely nonconstant localized signs
